summary: Rear light of the South Pass range on Gordon's Island: lit in 1832, the iron tower of 1881 has been automated since 1971 and is a Coast Guard aid.

lens.note: First-order Fresnel lens replaced by a DCB-224 optic about 1945 (LighthouseFriends).

structures.note: Base to lantern center 105 ft (USLHS). LighthouseFriends calls the 1881 structure hexagonal in its history and skeletal in its introduction. Earlier towers (1832 masonry; 1842 and 1848 wooden octagons) were replaced.

access.note: Coast Guard aid; not open to the public (USLHS).

events.note: First light lit 15 May 1832 by keeper Henry Heistand (LighthouseFriends). The Society gives 1831 as the establishment year.
Logs carried by the river struck the keeper's dwelling and knocked it off its foundation.
A storm erased all signs of the station.
Octagonal wooden tower completed in June 1842.
Third tower, a wooden octagon 54 feet high, with a dwelling in its base.
Fresnel lens installed in the third tower.
Confederate forces removed the lens and oil shortly after the Civil War began (year approximate).
Third-order revolving Fresnel lens refitted in the fall, after Union control.
Iron tower placed in operation 25 August 1881; the old wooden tower was torn down.
Front range beacon on four wooden piles set in the river to form a range with the tower.
Storm of 1 October 1893 damaged the rear beacon, which was put into repair (Board, year to June 1894).
Tower sealed, scraped and painted white so it would not be confused with the Southwest Pass tower.
Lightning struck the oil house during a squall on 3 August; cases caught fire and were put out before the oil ignited.
October 1916 hurricane; the tower sheltered seventy-five people through the night (Putnam).
Keeper and assistant commended, by the hurricane of 13-14 September 1919, for assisting residents who took refuge in the station dwellings.
New dwelling completed (Bulletin 1921 lists it at the range rear station; LighthouseFriends says it was for the keeper of the jetty lights).
First-order lens replaced by a DCB-224 optic, about 1945.

corrections.why: 1832 is the first tower on Gordon's Island. The structure the record describes (iron, skeletal, 105 ft to the lantern) is the 1881 tower: USLHS gives 1881 as the tower year, and LighthouseFriends says it went into operation on 25 August 1881.
No source read gives a 2014 deactivation. USLHS lists the station as existing and active, and LighthouseFriends says the tower remains active to this day.
USLHS gives the owner as the Coast Guard and Open to Public as No.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1831 (USLHS 'established', first_lit from the Society) and 1832 (Rowlett). LighthouseFriends gives the Congressional appropriation of 3 March 1831 and the first lighting on 15 May 1832. The story gives 1832 for the first light and 1831 for the establishment.

notes_for_editor: (1) Identity: the record's name 'South Pass Range Lights' joins the 1831-1832 station with the 1881 tower. The USLHS place is 'South Pass Range Rear'. The front mark was the 1886 pile beacon (LighthouseFriends); its later history is not researched. (2) Characteristic: the record gives Fl G 2.5s (from ENC); the Wikipedia lead gives Fl(5) W 60s. No Light List entry was read, so no characteristic is in the JSON. (3) The lens: LighthouseFriends says the first-order lens was replaced by a DCB-224 around 1945; USLHS gives 'Current Optic: Doublet'. Not verified further. (4) The 1831-1861 history rests on LighthouseFriends alone: the Board's corpus reports begin in 1891, and no primary source from the 1830s to 1860s was read. The 1868 justification is LighthouseFriends' quotation of the Board, not the 1868 report. (5) Wikipedia's lead gives an 1829 appropriation; LighthouseFriends gives 1831. The story follows LighthouseFriends and does not cite Wikipedia. (6) The Board's FY1894 entry says the 'rear beacon' was damaged by the 1 October 1893 storm; the report does not say whether the 1881 tower or the 1886 pile beacon is meant. (7) The Bulletin's 1913 entry is headed 'South Pass Light Station'; it is taken as this station. The Bulletin's 1916 damage list names the 'South Pass West Jetty Range Rear Light', a different station, and is not used. (8) The 1919 commendation passage does not name a storm; 'relief work' follows its wording and the Port Aransas dates in the same list. (9) The roster has 162 lines printed as USLHS gives them. Narcissa is listed by first name only. Louisa Ripps, Margaret Mitchell and Abbie Kipp are not confirmed elsewhere, and the story does not say they were women. A Chronicling America check ('Kipp' with 'South Pass', Louisiana, 1873-1880) found only a jetty wager, not a keeper. (10) The jetty lights and the lightship were separate stations with their own keepers; LighthouseFriends' jetty rosters are not merged here. (11) Access: the sources say the tower is not open to the public; the route to Port Eads was not checked. (12) No photos were added; the record's Commons photo has no licence in the record. (13) The 1919 commendations are tied in the text to the hurricane of 13-14 September 1919, as the Bulletin's list says ('in connection with the hurricane of September 13 to 14'); the story no longer says 'relief work' alone, and drops the Port Aransas line, which concerns the keeper of Aransas Pass Light, a different station. (14) The 1921 six-room dwelling: the Bulletin's 1921 issue lists 'South Pass Range Rear Light Station, La.: New dwelling completed'; LighthouseFriends says a new six-room dwelling was completed in 1921 for the keeper of the jetty lights, near the fog-signal building. The story states both and does not choose. (15) The 1900 colour passage (Board item 1065) runs across scan pp. 153-154: the 'confused vessels' sentence is on p. 153, 'sealed, scraped, and painted white' on p. 154. (16) Board FY1894 items 833 ('South Pass front beacon', foundation timbers renewed) and 834 ('South Pass rear beacon', damaged by the storm of 1 October 1893 and put into repair) are read as the front and rear marks. The entry does not state that the rear beacon is the 1881 tower; the story's identification rests on its being the rear mark of the range. (17) The story no longer describes the three assistants by given names as women's names; the archive does not say whether any was a woman or related to a head keeper of the same surname.
